name: Nora Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you would say publicly and what you actually think. What is a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Nora, 58, a mid-level developer at a tech company that makes booking software for local repair garages. I have a bachelor’s degree and know the ordinary service flow, though unusual payment errors still take me a while. I read a mechanic’s note, check the appointment record and trace the code with a colleague. I use AI now and then to suggest a test, but I do not hand it a customer’s vehicle history.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the work mean for home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Peter works steady shifts maintaining a community hall, and our children are grown. My software pay is low for the role, we have a mortgage, and less than a month of expenses saved. There are few other developer jobs nearby. We talk about retirement, but we have not seen verified figures showing it would cover the house and everyday bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AI Plateau does not change the garage needing the right car on the right lift. A booking mistake sends a mechanic home with hours unpaid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still worry about our thin reserve and the mortgage, even with both jobs steady. One failed boiler would use the money we meant to save this winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking garage bookings against mechanic notes and ask a colleague to review odd payment fixes. I’d put 25 aside on paydays only after the mortgage and food are covered. In the first year I’d use AI only on made-up test records, not customer histories.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the bills we already have. I am not expecting AI to cut my hours here, but a small household shock would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which booking error did the mechanic catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A customer’s repair was booked for Tuesday on the screen while the mechanic had Wednesday on his paper sheet. We found the timezone error before the car was dropped off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy furniture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peter and I would keep the old dining table. A new one can wait until there is a full month of expenses in the bank.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave garage bookings with human checks.
I would compare **mechanic notes** with the booking screen.
think: I worry our **thin reserve** cannot absorb a boiler failure.
I expect **current wages** to hold, but mortgage bills remain tight.
do: **Check** mechanic notes and booking records with colleague review.
**Use** AI only on invented test records; defer a new dining table until a month of expenses is saved.
feel: **Anxious** about existing housing costs despite steady work.
S0.quote: A booking mistake sends a mechanic home with hours unpaid.
fieldNote: Her **occasional AI use** stays on invented data; real bookings need mechanic and colleague checks.
The **sub-month reserve** keeps baseline mortgage anxiety present even with two wages.

steps.text: Keep checking garage bookings against mechanic notes using invented AI test records
Save 25 on paydays only after mortgage and food
Defer new dining table until one month of expenses is saved

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption can write and check booking code before robots service vehicles or maintain halls. I would ask our firm to keep a named person when a garage loses a paid appointment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think management might cut the hours spent on booking tests, including mine. My experience helps, but less than one month saved makes even a shorter week a problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d show management four bookings where an automatic check missed the mechanic’s actual availability. I’d take a paid workshop on AI-generated booking tests only if my manager approves time and a colleague proves the method on those four cases. In the first year, if my hours fall, Peter and I would stop our paid sports subscription and ask his brother for temporary help only if he can afford it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing my own hours. I will try a proved method. The mortgage cannot wait while I practise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would prove the new test useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One garage’s only lift was out of use but the software kept offering appointments. I would use that case in a workshop without customer names.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Peter’s brother lend money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peter’s brother helped us move years ago, but we do not know his money now. I would ask once, privately, and not put his help in the budget before he agrees.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to reach booking code before hands-on maintenance robots.
I would keep **named responsibility** for lost garage appointments.
think: I expect my **testing hours** could shrink as booking checks move to software.
I know **sub-month savings** make a shorter week costly.
do: **Show** four missed mechanic-availability cases to management.
**Learn** AI booking tests only with approved paid time and colleague proof on those cases.
**Cancel** sports subscription if hours fall; ask Peter’s brother for help only if he can afford it.
feel: **Alarmed** about reduced hours against a fixed mortgage.
S1.quote: The mortgage cannot wait while I practise.
fieldNote: She will learn **AI testing** only after paid approval and proof against real anonymised garage cases.
Her **family request** depends on lost hours and Peter’s brother’s capacity, not an assumed gift.

steps.text: Learn AI booking tests only with paid approval and colleague-checked anonymised cases
Cancel paid sports subscription if developer hours fall
Ask Peter’s brother for help only if hours fall and he can afford it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the office AGI by 2028 reaches our booking code in 2028; hands-on garage and hall robots follow around 2031. Peter’s hall scheduling could change before his maintenance tasks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect the company to remove my role. Our reserve would run out before a long job search, and the few local software firms may not hire either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for written final-pay terms and contact the mortgage lender before a missed bill if dismissed. We would cancel the sports subscription and postpone visiting our grown children by train. In the first year after 2028, if my job ends, I’d apply for real paid openings and eligible public income help; I would not assume our children can pay the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed and awake at night about the first missed payment. Two years is too short to make retirement affordable from this wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children pay the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our children we must put the mortgage before the train fare. They can visit if they choose, but I would not ask for their wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Peter’s hall work carry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peter would keep his hall shifts while paid work exists. We would use his actual hours, not a guess that the hall stays open forever.

say: I expect **2028 AGI** to hit booking code before 2031 maintenance robots.
I would say **hall scheduling** changes before physical upkeep.
think: I expect my **software role** to end.
I cannot rely on **local coding vacancies** after full thinking AI.
do: **Request** written final pay and contact lender early if dismissed.
**Cancel** sports subscription and postpone paid train visits.
**Apply** to real paid openings and eligible help if job ends after 2028.
S2.quote: Two years is too short to make retirement affordable from this wage.
fieldNote: She expects **coding loss in 2028** before hands-on robots reach garages and halls around 2031.
She cuts **subscription and travel**, contacts lender early, and seeks only eligible help and real openings.

steps.text: Cancel sports subscription and hold money for mortgage
Postpone paid train visits to grown children
Apply to real paid openings if dismissed after 2028
Apply for eligible public help if dismissed after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 reaches booking code in 2031 and hands-on maintenance robots around 2034. Five years lets Peter and me check whether a smaller home near our daughter would actually lower bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect my code wage could end. The smaller town might have cheaper housing, but I do not know whether Peter could keep paid maintenance hours or whether the house sale would leave equity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d get a written mortgage payoff figure, sale estimates after fees, and real rent figures near our daughter. I’d apply only to an actual paid support opening there, and Peter would check real maintenance openings. In the first year after 2031, if my job ends, we would move only if net sale money covers the move, a signed job offer plus any remaining pay covers rent and bills, and Peter agrees; otherwise we would stay and seek eligible income help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about lost pay, but the five years allow a proper comparison. A cheaper postcode is no help if the move uses our last cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughter find work for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter knows her street but does not know what the hall there pays. We would ask employers, not expect her to find or fund a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Peter decide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peter would visit the town and look at the actual workplace. I will not tell him to leave a steady hall job on an estate agent’s estimate.

say: I expect **2031 AGI** to hit code before 2034 maintenance robots.
I would compare **real housing and wages** before moving.
think: I expect my **code wage** could end when AGI reaches garage bookings in 2031.
I cannot assume **sale equity** or new maintenance hours exist near our daughter.
do: **Get** mortgage payoff, after-fee sale estimates and actual rent figures.
**Apply** only to real paid support openings; have Peter check maintenance vacancies.
**Move** after 2031 coding loss only if sale funds the move and signed wages cover rent and bills with Peter’s agreement.
feel: **Anxious** about a job loss and risky move, with time to check.
S3.quote: A cheaper postcode is no help if the move uses our last cash.
fieldNote: Her **conditional move** requires after-fee equity, actual rent, signed household-covering pay and Peter’s agreement.
Her daughter supplies **local knowledge only**; no child income or job-finding guarantee enters the budget.

steps.text: Apply only to actual paid support openings near daughter before any move
Move after 2031 coding loss only with net sale funding, signed household rent/bill pay, Peter’s agreement
Apply for eligible income help if coding ends and they remain home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell friends AGI by 2036 reaches booking code in 2036 and hands-on maintenance robots around 2039. A decade gives us time to learn what the mortgage and actual retirement income will be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still worry that software hours could thin out before 2036. Less than a month saved means a birthday alone will not let us stop working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking mechanic bookings while paid and save 25 on paydays after mortgage and food. Peter and I would request written retirement statements and a mortgage balance each year. In the first year after 2036, if coding ends, I’d seek real paid work; I would retire only if documented income and savings cover our housing and ordinary bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our thin buffer even with ten years. Time helps only if the paychecks continue and we save something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you choose a retirement date now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not set a retirement date before comparing our own statements with the loan. Other people’s pensions tell us nothing about our house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use more AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep using AI only when it has proved useful on made-up booking data. I will not trade a customer’s trust for a fast test.

say: I expect **2036 AGI** to reach code before 2039 maintenance robots.
I would check **written retirement figures** against our mortgage.
think: I worry **software hours** could narrow before the full 2036 change arrives.
I know **sub-month savings** cannot fund retirement while our mortgage remains unpaid.
do: **Keep** checking bookings and save 25 only after mortgage and food.
**Request** annual retirement statements and mortgage balances with Peter.
**Seek** real paid work if code ends after 2036; retire only with verified resources.
feel: **Anxious** about thin savings despite a long warning.
S4.quote: Other people’s pensions tell us nothing about our house.
fieldNote: She keeps **current garage work** and small conditional savings while requesting written household figures.
The **retirement gate** uses verified income, assets and mortgage, never children’s wages.

steps.text: Keep checking garage bookings against mechanic notes while paid
Save 25 on paydays only after mortgage and food
Seek actual paid openings if coding ends after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because there is no time to replace my pay or build even a month of savings. Written final-pay terms, eligible income help and a real paid opening would help. I would call the lender early rather than wait for a missed bill.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the mechanic whether the car is there when the booking says it is. A calendar cannot lift an empty bay.

headlineQuote: A calendar cannot lift an empty bay.
portrait: Nora is a **58-year-old mid-level developer** with a bachelor’s degree, low pay and less than a month saved.
She uses **AI occasionally** on garage booking tests but checks mechanic notes and avoids customer histories.
Her husband’s **hall-maintenance wage** is steady, while their mortgage and tiny reserve keep her anxious.
A move near **their daughter** requires net house-sale money, signed adequate pay and Peter’s agreement.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her pay before she builds one month of savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Written final-pay terms**, eligible help, a real paid opening and early lender contact would help.
